document.full_text:
Several laboratories have reported that guanosine 5'-triphosphate (GTP) and more than one enzyme fraction are involved in the transfer of amino acids from amino acyl-RNA to ribosome-bound polypeptides (1). Our work using a cell-free system from rabbit reticulocytes has revealed that two soluble enzyme fractions and GTP are needed for the formation of small polypeptides of phenylalanine from phenylalanyl-RNA in the presence of poly U (polyuridylic acid) (2). In a preliminary note we have reported that these same enzyme fractions are necessary for the transfer of leucine-14C from leucyl-14C RNA into polypeptides using a reticulocyte system in the absence of poly U (3). This transfer system was shown previously to synthesize soluble hemoglobin under optimal conditions (4). Here we describe in detail the methods used in isolation of the purified enzyme fractions and the general properties of this hemoglobin transfer system.
EXPERIMENTAL METHODS
(a) (NH&SOa fractionation. Rabbits were made anemic with phenylhydrazine, and the reticulocytes were collected and lysed as previously described (5). Figure 1 shows a general scheme for the purification of the enzyme fractions. The solution from the 68,000g centrifugation of the reticulocyte lysate was stored at -15" until used. About 1700 ml of this supernatant fraction were thawed overnight at 5", and neutralized protamine sulfate (10 mg/ml) was added to a final After stirring for 30 minutes, the suspension was centrifuged, and the supernatant phase was discarded.
The precipitate was dissolved in 850 ml of 0.10 M Tris-HCl, pH 6.5 at 0", containing 1 mu glutathione (GSH) and 0. T to decarboxylate the free amino acids, and the liberated CO2 was trapped for analysis of radioactivity (10).
Ribosome and enzyme preparations. Enzyme activity for transferring amino acid from aminoacyl-RN-4 to polypeptide was measured in a reaction mixture containing ribosomes washed with a KC1 solution (see METHODS). Table I shows that addition of a crude enzyme fraction to a system containing unwashed ribosomes provided only a and reisolated by centrifugation.

Suspension of t'he unwashed ribosomes in medium B (see METHODS) followed by centrifugation removed much of this enzyme activity (Table I). However, oth.er experiments revealed th.at these ribosomes were still inadequate for demonstrating a requirement, for both of the purified enzymes TF-1 and TF-2 in a transfer assay. Significant amounk of the TF-2 fraction were bound very tightly to the ribosomes. Washing t)hp ribosomes with 0.10 M KC1 in medium B removed this remaining enzyme activity. A transfer reaction using these ribosomes now required added enzyme fractions (Table I). Others have reported that crude ribosome fractions isolated from li:scherichia coli and rat liver have transfer enzyme activities which can be removed by washing with salts or desoxycholate ( 11,12).
The preparat'ion of the two transfer fractions was modified from that' briefly reported earlier (3) in order bo improve the yield and separation. The procedure (Fig. 1) consists of a protamine sulfate treatment of the reticulocyte soluble phase to remove sRNA, an (NH&S04 fractionation, and a partial separation of the t,wo enzyme activities using a calcium phosphate gel. Further purification of the two fractions was obtained by chromatography on DEAEcellulose columns.
Fractionation of the 78,OOOg supernatant phase of the cell with (NH&S04 increased the enzyme specific activity for transfer about la-fold (Table II). The ammonium sulfate fraction contained all the soluble enzymes needed t,o incorporate amino acids into hemoglobin, including the aminoacyl-RNA synthetases (.i), but most of the hemoglobin in the cell lysate had been removed. Further purification using a calcium phosphat'e gel removed almost all of the remaining hemoglobin in the discarded S-l fraction (Fig. 1). Gel fraction S-2 contained the peptide synt'het'ase enzyme (TIT-2) and was devoid of the binding enzyme (TF-1). Hence, the S-2 fraction alone could not catalyze transfer of leucine-14C into polypeptides (Table II). Gel fraction S-3 COIItained the binding enzyme and significant amounts of the peptide synthetase; this crude fraction had a speci'tic activity for transfer 3040 times th.at of the 78,OOOg supernatant phase (Table II).
The specific activkies of the purified fractions TF-1 and TF-2 were not measured in the experiments shown in Table II, because separately they did not stimulate transfer. However, other assays revealed t,hat the TF-1 fract'ion catalyzed t)he transfer of about, 400~~moles of leuc'ine-14C per milligram of enzyme protein when saturating amounts of the TF-2 fraction and 3 mg of ribosomes were used. Conversely, the TF-2 fraction catalyzed the transfer of about 600 ppmoles of leucine-14C per milligram of enzyme protein when t,he TF-1 fraction was present in excess.
Furthermore, the specific activity of the TF-1 fraction for the binding of phenylalanyl-RNA to ribosomes in t,he presence of poly U (2) was found to be loo-fold great'er than that of the 7S,OOOg supernatant phase for the total transfer of phenylalanine. In this poly U system t'he amount of phenylalanine kansferred in the presence of both fractions TF-1 and TF-2 was always greater than the amount of phenylalanyl-RNA bound to the ribosomes with TF-1 alone.
Although the binding activity of the crude supernatant phase could not be measured directly because of the contaminating peptide synthetase, these results suggest that the binding activity was purified at least loo-fold in the preparation of the TF-1 fraction. Too, in other assays the TF-1 fraction did not contain phenylalanyl-RNA synthetase activity.
Requirements for the transfer reaction. Transfer of amino acids from aminoacyl-RNA into polypeptides required both enzyme fractions TF-1 and TF-2 (Fig. 2; Table III). The usual synergism was six to ten times the sum of the separate incorporations catalyzed by each fraction alone. When either enzyme fraction was heated briefly at 100" and then used with the complementary enzyme, there was no incorporation.
Table III shows that transfer of leucine-14C into polypeptides required GSH. We had reported earlier that GSH was required to preserve enzyme activity for transfer in studies using a crude ammonium sulfate fraction (13). In the present studies this requirement was demonstrated only if the TF-2 fraction was freed of GSH and EDTA and stored frozen in their absence. There was still activity for transfer when the TF-2 fraction was freed of GSH and used immediately in an assay without GSH. Thus, a sulfhydryl compound is needed in the transfer assay presumably to keep the TF-2 fraction in an active state. Hardesty and coworkers have reached a similar conclusion in their studies with a reticulocyte transfer system (14). Sutter and Moldave have reported also that GSH activates only one of the two transfer fractions in a system from rat liver ( 15).
The requirements for ilIgC1, (Table III) and KC1 in the transfer reaction were almost absolute. Figure 3a sh.ows that a concentration of 1.5-2.5 mM i\IgCl, was optimal for the transfer reaction. The optimal concentration of KC1 was about, 100 m&f (Fig. 3b). These concentrations of MgClz and KC1 are very similar to those of the cell-free system incorporating free amino acids into hemoglobin (5). Hence, these data are consistent with the hypoth.esis that the transfer syst,em is incorporating amino acids into globin polypeptides.
Table III also shows that GTP was rcquired for the transfer of amino acids into polypeptides, as has been reported for other transfer systems. Maximum transfer required concentrations of 20 PM GTP or greater. Table IV shows that other nucleoside triphosphates and GDP were relatively inactive in stimulating transfer. Such specificity for GTP was found only if the aminoacyl-14C-RNA preparations were passed through columns of Sephadex G-25 in order to remove small amounts or" contaminating nucleoside triphosphates (see METHODS).
In the presence of a11 optimal amount of GTP, addition of ATP, or creatine phosphate w&h creatine kinase did not, increase incorporation.

The transfer of 14C-amino acid from aminoacyl-RNA to polypeptides reached a maximum after three minutes of incubation at 37"; no transfer occurred at 0". 60 50 \ Ribosonte-bound prodz~cts. All synthesized 14C-polypeptides were bound to the ribosomes when they were centrifuged from one of the transfer assays. This finding is attributed to the limiting amounts of amino-acyLRNA used in the assays. Moreover, some additional radioactive products were bound t'o the isolated ribosomes. These products would not precipit)ate with trichloroacetic acid after th.e ribosome residue had been dissolved in KaOH (see NETHODS). Such acid-soluble products normally were discarded during the acid washes used to prepare 14C-polypeptides for the analysis of radioact,ivity, because t'he xvash procedure (3) included a step in which the residue bvas treated \vith KaOH. The acid-soluble products contjained about 30% of the total radioact)ivity bound to the ribosomes (Table V). Tbey are presumably amino acids and small pept,ides wh.ich were originally attached through ester bonds to sRNA molecules on the ribosomes.
A substantial percentage of the product)s of a poly U-stimulat,ed transfer system were found previously to be phenylalanyl-RSA molecules bound to tb.e ribosomes (2). It n-as of interest) t,o know what percentage of tb.e ribosome-bound radioactivity in the hemoglobin transfer system could be identified as amino acyl-RNA.
For these experiments v~~~I-'~C~RNA containing valine labeled with. 14C in only the carbon atom of the carboxyl group was used. After a transfer incubation the labeled ribosomes were isolated by centrifugation.
About 305% of the total radioactivity bound to the ribosomes was extracted in th.e acid-soluble fraction described in t,he preceding paragraph. Th.ese product's lvere treated with chloramine T in a procedure which decarboxylates onl\ free amino acids and collects the liberated-14C02 (10). About, 12 % of the mat,erial n-as found to be free valine-14C using this procedure, and the rest n-as presumably small peptides. Thus, of t,he total product bound to the ribosome, about 70% of the radio-activit,y n'as incorporated into polypcptides large enough to precipitate nith t'richloroacetic acid, 26 % NXS in small peptides soluble in acid, and only 4 o/c could be identified as amino acyl-RKA.
Although the exact nature of t'he acid soluble peptides is unknown, the percentage of radioactivity in this fraction remained the same \\-hen leucyl-14C-RSA or phenylalanyl-14C-RSA, instead of valylJ4C-RSA, was used in the reaction. Therefore, it is doubtful that, the small peptides represent, newly started ch.ains containing the first fern amino acids coded by mRXA for hemoglobin, because t,here arc 110 phenylalanine residues near the amino terminus of either rabbit hemoglobin chain (16,17). Perhaps they represent an artifact ph.enomenon involving ribosomes isolat,ed in the process of cb.ain elongation which have lost ;I peptidyl-RXA during the preparative procedures; in this case, synthesis reinitiat,ed in the cellfree system might produce some small labeled pept'ides coded by se&ions of mRNA other t#han those corresponding to the aminot'erminal ends of the complete chains.
Only one of the transfer enzymes, the TF-1 fraction, is needed to stimulate the binding of phenylalanyl-RLNA to ribosomes in the polg C kansfer system (see Ih-CUSSIOS). An attempt was made to det'ect a similar react'ion in the hemoglobin trsnsfcr system.
Holyever, Table V sholvs that substantial amounts of the acid-soluble product's, including possible aminoacyl-RNA molecules, were found only when both transfer enzymes were used. Thus, in cont'rast) to the poly U transfer q&em, t'he TIC-1 fraction does not, stimulate the binding of sizable amounts of aminoacyl-RNA to the ribosomes in t)he hemoglobin transfer system.
We have reported previously that t,hc TIC-1 and TP-2 enzyme fra&ons stimulate t'he formation of polyphenylalanine from phenylalanyl-RKA in the presence of poly U and ribosomes devoid of hemoglobin mRNA (2). In this poly U system the TIC-1 fract'ion and GTI' stimulat,ed the binding of phenylalanyl-RSA to t'he ribosomes, while t'he TF-2 fraction catalyzed t,he formation of the peptide bond of plieri?-lal:IIlr-lphel~~l:~l:lrlillc, in isolated reactions. Thus, these enzymes catalyze at least two sequental steps in polypeptide synthesis. When both enzymes were used in the same reaction mixture only 20 % of the ribosome-bound radioactivity was located in polyphenylalanine molecules having a sufficient number of residues to be precipitable with trich.loroacetic acid after NaOH treatment. The majority of the ribosome-bound products were oligopeptides too small to precipitate with acid. We suggest that the ability of the TF-1 fraction alone to stimulate the binding of phenylalanyl-RNA to the ribosomes and the preponderance of small peptides formed in the presence of both enzymes are manifestations of a system in which polypeptide chains are being initiated.
Conversely, in the transfer system documented in this report, about 70% of the ribosome-bound radioactivity was precipitable with trichloroacetic acid after NaOH treatment.
This finding is consistent with the hypothesis that amino acids were incorporated into polypeptide chains which were interrupted in growth by cell lysis. We can only speculate about the reason for failure of one enzyme fraction with GTP to stimulate the binding of aminoacyl-RNA in this hemoglobin transfer system. Probably only a few globin chains, if any, are initiated in the reaction incubation. However, during the growth of existing polypeptide chains, the ribosome is thought to have at least two binding sites, one for peptidyl-RNA and one for the aminoacyl-RNA bearing the amino acid to be added to the growing chain (18,19). If both of these sites are already occupied on the ribosomes added to the reaction mixture, it may be necessary for the peptide synthetase (TF-2) to catalyze peptide bond formation and th.e TF-1 fraction to catalyze a translocation of the new peptidyl-RNA (20) before a site is available for the binding of aminoacyl-RNA.
In this event GTP and the TF-1 fraction presumably catalyze a reaction other than the physical binding of phenylalanyl-RNA, as discussed in th.e following paper (21). In t'he poly U system, ph.enylalanyl-RNA can bind to ribosomes containing chains of polyphenylalanine, but the available sites are thought to be ('primed" by the prior incubation of these ribosomes with the transfer enzymes (20). Conversely, in the present transfer system a binding site may be available, but the complex formed is unstable to isolation by centrifugation.
Our studies with the two types of transfer systems using reticulocyte ribosomes have demonstrated that conventional methods of product preparation for analysis of incorporated radioactivity may give misleading results. These methods include a step in which the acid-precipitated protein is heated at 90" (22) or suspended in NaOH (5). These procedures remove the radioactivity in aminoacyl-RNA molecules from the polypeptide residue. Our work shows, however, that not only amino acids, but also those radioactive peptides too small to precipitate with acid, are removed. Thus, investigations studying ch.ain initiation may not' be able to use these conventional techniques to dedetermine formation of the first peptide bond(s) .
